title: The corner of the field (Mishnah Peah)
hook: how much to leave for the poor, and who may gather it

segments.voice: Yesterday, why blessings come first, and your line: thanks before the harvest. What did you pause to thank for before you took it? Today, the harvest itself, and the part that isn't the farmer's. Day one thousand seventy.

The wheat is down across the whole field except one end. There, a strip of grain still stands, gold and untouched, as if the reapers forgot it. They didn't. The farmer's work is finished, and he's gone home. Later, people come with their own sickles, people who own no field at all, and they cut it themselves. Nobody hands it to them. Nobody picks who gets some. It's theirs by right. The Torah asks for this strip. The Mishnah has a whole tractate on it, and it starts asking the questions a real farmer would ask. How big? And who gets to take it?
screen: `ONE END OF THE FIELD STILL STANDING.` → `THEY CUT IT THEMSELVES.` → `HOW BIG? WHO TAKES IT?`

segments.voice: The corner of the field. In Hebrew, peah. The Torah's command, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "thou shalt not wholly reap the corner of thy field." Leave it, it says, for the poor and for the stranger. It never says how much. So the Mishnah, in tractate Peah, asks. First it admits the Torah set no measure. Then it sets a floor: a person should not leave less than one sixtieth. And it adds that the right amount depends on the size of the field, the number of the poor, and how good the harvest was. A floor, but no ceiling. A big year and a crowd of hungry people should mean a bigger corner. The second question is just as important: who gathers it? The Mishnah says the corner is given while the grain is still standing in the ground, and the poor reap it themselves. The farmer doesn't cut it and hand it out to people he likes. There are exceptions, like grapes on high trellises and dates at the top of tall palms, and there the owner brings the fruit down and divides it. But the rule is that the corner isn't the farmer's gift. It belongs to the poor, and they come and take what is theirs. And near its close, the tractate turns to the one who takes. In paraphrase: whoever takes without needing to will not leave the world before coming to need others. And whoever truly needs, and holds back from taking, will live to support others from their own. The corner is for the ones who need it, and the Mishnah asks the one who takes to be honest about that.
screen: `PEAH: THE TORAH GIVES NO SIZE.` · `NO LESS THAN A SIXTIETH; NO CEILING.` · `THE POOR REAP IT THEMSELVES.` · `TAKE ONLY IF YOU NEED.` · then, large: `THE CORNER.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: leave a portion for someone. Sit with the bell and think about one thing you'll have plenty of today. Food in the fridge. Time on your calendar. Money in an account. Patience, maybe. Picture its corner: the part you could leave standing for someone else. Don't decide yet who will get it. That's the point of the corner. Just picture setting it aside, and then decide how you'll leave it where someone who needs it can reach it, without having to ask. The bell holds the time.
The corner of the field. Peah: the edge of the harvest left standing for the poor, at least a sixtieth, and reaped by the poor themselves. Today's word.
screen: `THE CORNER OF THE FIELD — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the corner. Today, leave one corner of something you have where someone who needs it can take it, without you choosing who. Day one thousand seventy.

howItsDone: Jewish law treats the corner of the field as the poor's by right; where farming laws are kept in the land of Israel, some farmers still leave peah, and Jewish teachers draw on these laws when describing giving that protects the dignity of the one who receives.

fork.setup: you're a farmer. the harvest is in, except the corner. a poor neighbor you like is nearby, and so are strangers. what does the Mishnah say happens?
options: cut it and give it to the neighbor you like.
leave it standing; the poor come and reap it themselves.
sell it and give the money away.
fork.reveal: the corner is given while still attached to the ground, and the poor reap it themselves. it isn't the farmer's to hand out.

original.note: Hebrew: corner, edge; the corner of the field left for the poor, and the name of the tractate.

trapdoor: what you thought: leave some leftovers for the poor if you can.
what it means: the corner of the field belongs to the poor by right. at least a sixtieth, and they reap it themselves.
what a scholar hears: Peah 1:2's floor that rises with field, poor and yield; 4:1's rule that the poor take it from the ground; and 8:9's teaching on taking only in need.

notes: Days 150 and 547 used Peah 1:1 (things without measure; study of Torah); this day avoids it and takes the outline's two questions, how much and who gathers.
Leviticus 19:9 quoted from JPS 1917 ('thou shalt not wholly reap the corner of thy field'). Please confirm.
Mishnah Peah 1:2 paraphrased: not less than one sixtieth, and the amount depends on the size of the field, the number of poor and the yield. The 'sixtieth' is the text's own number. Please confirm.
Mishnah Peah 4:1 paraphrased: peah is given from what is attached to the ground; for hanging vines (dalit) and date palms the owner takes it down and distributes. Please confirm.
